raw_case_text:
A 5-week-old female presented to hospital with 3 days of diarrhea, poor feeding, decreased activity, and two episodes of unilateral leg shaking that self-resolved in less than 1 min. of 2 weeks prior, she had 1 day of fever. She had no respiratory symptoms, vomiting, rash, or decreased level of consciousness.
The infant's mother migrated from Nigeria 9 years prior. This pregnancy was conceived during travel to Nigeria. The mother returned to Canada at 5-months gestation. Testing for HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis was negative at 7-months gestation.
The infant was delivered by caesarean section at 37 + 5 weeks gestation for breech presentation. The mother had fever at delivery and on post-operative day one, then defervesced without antibiotics. The baby's birth weight was 3.1 kg. Neonatal examination was normal. She fed and gained weight appropriately until the current illness.
In the Emergency Department (ED), the infant was afebrile, with vital signs in normal range. Examination revealed lethargy and a soft flow murmur. Hemoglobin was 64 g/L, hematocrit 20%, white blood cells 8.5 x 109/L, platelets 331 x 109/L, and glucose 5.2 mmol/L.
The Hematology technician contacted the ED to report having seen malaria parasites (at 0.1% parasitemia) on the blood smear performed for complete blood count with manual differential. Rapid diagnostic test for malaria (BinaxNOW; Abbott, Chicago, IL, USA) was done and was negative.
Further history revealed that the mother was treated for malaria at 6-weeks' gestation in Nigeria (see case timeline in Supplemental Figure 1). She did not know the causative species or medication. Fever recurred at 6-months gestation in Canada. The mother contacted her physician in Nigeria, who advised to take a course of antimalarial therapy she had brought back from Nigeria. Fever resolved.
The infant was transferred to the pediatric hospital and the Infectious Diseases service was consulted. The infant was alert but pale, and noted to have tachycardia, retractions, and desaturations with feeding. Hepatosplenomegaly was palpated. Hemoglobin was 55 g/L, hematocrit 17.3%, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Liver panel, creatinine, and C-reactive protein were normal.
Red blood cells were transfused due to symptomatic anemia. Congenital malaria was presumed given absence of endemic malaria transmission in Canada, and managed as a severe case given progressive anemia and possible seizures. IV artesunate was initiated (3.0 mg/kg/dose at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h). Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were started pending full septic workup. Repeat peripheral blood smear confirmed 0.1% parasitemia, and Plasmodium ovale was identified by microscopy and polymerase chain reaction at the provincial reference laboratory.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-week-old female infant presenting with diarrhea, poor feeding, decreased activity, and brief unilateral leg shaking episodes for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 5-week-old female infant presented with a three-day history of loose stools, poor feeding, decreased activity, and two self-limiting episodes of unilateral leg shaking each lasting under one minute. Two weeks prior, she had experienced a single day of fever. She was brought to the emergency department where anemia and lethargy were noted, prompting transfer to a tertiary pediatric intensive care unit for progressive respiratory distress and pallor during feeds.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born at 37+5 weeks gestation via Cesarean section for breech presentation (birth weight 3.1 kg, normal neonatal exam) to a mother who immigrated from Nigeria 9 years prior and traveled to Nigeria during pregnancy (conception in Nigeria, return to Canada at 5 months gestation). Mother was treated for malaria at 6 weeks gestation in Nigeria, experienced recurrent fever at 6 months gestation treated with self-administered Nigerian antimalarials, and had peripartum fever. Mother tested negative for HIV, HBV, and syphilis at 7 months gestation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for poor feeding, lethargy, diarrhea, and brief unilateral focal shaking. Negative for vomiting, cough, rhinorrhea, rash, or decreased level of consciousness. Medications: none. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: In emergency department: afebrile, vital signs normal; lethargic with a soft systolic flow murmur. Upon transfer to pediatric ICU: alert but marked pallor, tachycardia, subcostal retractions and oxygen desaturations during feeding. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Emergency department labs: hemoglobin 64 g/L, hematocrit 20%, white blood cells 8.5 x 10^9/L, platelets 331 x 10^9/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L. Pediatric hospital labs: hemoglobin 55 g/L, hematocrit 17.3%, lactate 2.1 mmol/L; normal hepatic transaminases, normal creatinine, and normal C-reactive protein. Rapid diagnostic test (BinaxNOW) was negative. Peripheral blood smear performed for complete blood count with manual differential.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe congenital Plasmodium ovale malaria complicated by severe progressive hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin nadir 55 g/L), feeding desaturations, hepatosplenomegaly, and suspected focal seizures.
Diagnostic confirmation: Routine CBC blood smear manual differential identifying intraerythrocytic parasites at 0.1% parasitemia (false-negative BinaxNOW rapid diagnostic test); repeat smear confirmed 0.1% parasitemia, and Plasmodium ovale was definitively identified by reference laboratory light microscopy and species-specific PCR. Full septic workup was negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with emergency packed red blood cell transfusion for symptomatic severe anemia, intravenous artesunate (3.0 mg/kg/dose at 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours), and empiric IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir pending microbiological culture and viral results.
